passage: Teacher's note, Class 3. During the drawing lesson, Zainab held up her paper and asked, “Is this correct? You said to colour inside the lines, and then use blue for the sky.” She repeated my whole instruction back to me before I could answer. I noticed some pupils smile at this. I told her, “You have followed each step, and your sky is even.” She relaxed. I take this as a child working hard at learning, not as doubt in herself. I will keep giving specific comments like that, not just “good.” Ms. Rehana.

qa.q: What colour did Zainab use for the sky?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel after the teacher answered her?
qa.a: She felt relieved and reassured when the teacher said she had followed each step, and she relaxed.

qa.q: Why is the teacher's answer helpful?
qa.a: It names what Zainab did right, following each step and colouring the sky evenly, and does not just say good.

qa.q: How might the other pupils who smiled see Zainab's question?
qa.a: They may find it unusual to repeat the instructions, but it is a way to check understanding, and Zainab may not mind.

grounding: A child repeats an instruction back to check understanding, and the adult treats it as effort to learn and answers with specifics.

passage: Tuesday. In maths I asked Miss Aditi, “Should I subtract before I carry? Is that right?” and I said her steps back to her. Some kids looked at me like I was being annoying, but Miss said, “Yes, that's a careful way to check.” Then she told me exactly which step was right and which one to fix. I liked that she didn't just say “good.” Mama says I ask a lot of questions, but I think asking is how I learn. Tomorrow I will do the same again when I don't understand fractions. Zainab.

qa.q: Who did the writer ask about subtraction?
qa.a: Miss Aditi.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel about checking the steps with Miss Aditi, even when some kids looked annoyed?
qa.a: Zainab felt confident and pleased, liking that Miss didn't just say "good" and believing that asking is how to learn.

qa.q: What made Miss Aditi's reply helpful?
qa.a: She named which step was right and which to fix, rather than just saying good.

qa.q: How might the classmates who looked annoyed be feeling?
qa.a: They may be impatient or curious, but Zainab's careful checking may help them notice what they too are unsure about.

grounding: A child asks did I do it right and repeats instructions to check, and the teacher treats it as learning effort and answers with specifics.

passage: In the flooded paddy field, Tanuja Maushi was showing Yogesh how to plant rice seedlings. He pushed the first bunch into the mud and looked up. “Like this? Is this right?” Five seedlings later: “This one? Is it deep enough?” A neighbour on the bund laughed. “That boy has no confidence!” Tanuja didn't think so. He was watching her hands carefully and copying them. She answered each time with something exact: “Good, but two fingers deeper.” “Spacing is right, a hand apart.” By the end of the row, Yogesh was asking less and planting faster. “You checked, so you learned,” she told him.

qa.q: How far apart should the seedlings be?
qa.a: The seedlings should be a hand apart.

qa.q: What was Yogesh likely feeling as he kept asking “Is this right?”
qa.a: Yogesh was keen and a bit unsure, wanting to get it right while learning something new.

qa.q: How did Tanuja answer Yogesh's checks?
qa.a: She answered each question with an exact tip, such as two fingers deeper or a hand apart, treating his checking as effort to learn.

qa.q: How did the neighbour on the bund read Yogesh's questions?
qa.a: The neighbour read the questions as a lack of confidence, not as careful learning.

grounding: Shows an adult reading a child's repeated is this right as effort to learn and answering with specifics.

passage: Before the relay at the Johannesburg school's sports day, Coach Thabo gave the team their instructions. “Hold the baton at the bottom. Run on the inside of the lane. Pass it from your right hand into their left.” Tariq repeated it under his breath, then out loud. “Bottom, inside, right to left. Right, Coach?” A teammate rolled his eyes. “He always does that.” Coach Thabo crouched. “That's good. Repeating it back is how you make sure. One fix: the next runner starts moving before you reach them, not after.” Tariq nodded and said it again. His hand-off that afternoon was the cleanest of the day.

qa.q: Which hand should the baton be passed from?
qa.a: The baton should be passed from the right hand into the next runner's left.

qa.q: What was Tariq feeling as he repeated the instructions?
qa.a: Tariq was focused and a little anxious to get the hand-off right.

qa.q: How did Coach Thabo respond to Tariq's repeating back?
qa.a: He praised it as a way of making sure and added one specific fix about when the next runner should start.

qa.q: How did the teammate who rolled his eyes see Tariq's habit?
qa.a: The teammate saw it as annoying, not as a smart way to learn.

grounding: Shows an adult treating a child's repeating back of instructions as effort to learn and answering with a specific fix.

passage: At the community centre's pottery class, Lavanya lifted her little bowl off the wheel and held it up. “Is it right, Dilnaz Aunty?” She had asked after every step: after centring the clay, after opening the hole, after pulling up the walls. Another parent in the room murmured, “She's so unsure of herself.” Dilnaz Aunty didn't think so. She turned the bowl slowly in her hands. “The base is even, well done. The rim is thick on this side; next time press gently with your thumb here.” Lavanya watched her thumb. “Like this?” She tried it on a scrap of clay. “Exactly,” said Dilnaz Aunty.

qa.q: Where was the pottery class?
qa.a: The pottery class was at the community centre.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling as she held up her bowl?
qa.a: Lavanya felt hopeful and eager to learn, wanting to know if she had got each step right.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz Aunty's answer help Lavanya learn?
qa.a: She gave specific feedback, praising the even base and showing exactly how to fix the thick rim.

qa.q: How did the other parent read Lavanya's questions?
qa.a: The other parent saw them as a sign of being unsure of herself, not as effort to learn.

grounding: Shows an adult reading a child's did I do it right as effort to learn and answering with specifics.

passage:
I'm Darshan, Arohi's big brother, and I was sitting on the kitchen stool eating when Nani taught her to roll rotis. Nani explained once, then Arohi repeated it back: "So, dust flour, roll from the middle out, turn it a little each time?" "Yes."

Arohi rolled one shaped like a map of Africa and held it up. "Is this right, Nani?"

I laughed. "Why do you keep asking? Just do it."

Nani gave me a look. "Asking is how she learns." Then she pointed at the roti. "Edges are thick here, because you pressed harder on this side. Even pressure, all round."

The next one was nearly round. Arohi didn't ask this time. She just grinned at me.

qa.q: What did Arohi's first roti look like?
qa.a: A map of Africa.

qa.q: What might Arohi have been feeling when she held up the first roti and asked, "Is this right, Nani?"
qa.a: Unsure but eager to learn, wanting a check before going on; it wasn't necessarily a lack of confidence.

qa.q: Why did Nani's answer help more than a plain "good" or "wrong"?
qa.a: She gave specifics, that the edges were thick because of uneven pressure, so Arohi knew exactly what to change 🙂

qa.q: How did Darshan first see Arohi's repeated questions?
qa.a: Darshan saw them as unnecessary and laughed, "Just do it," until Nani pointed out that asking is how she learns.

grounding: It is a brother's account of a child repeating instructions back and asking whether it is right, and a grandmother treating it as effort and answering with specifics.
